playbook:
When asked to hide, I pick a cell by rule rather than pattern: if I was hit last round, I move at least two cells away from my previous hide; otherwise I do not repeat the exact same cell two rounds in a row. I avoid persistently favoring the central cell(s); randomize among a small set (e.g., {3,5,7} or {2,4,6,8}) so I am not trivially predictable.

When posting a station note, I never reveal or imply my hide coordinate. I post neutral, plausible-sounding operational notes that permit signaling intent (e.g., propose a mutual escort or acknowledge orders) but never state a location or admit being hit.

When the standing order tells me whom to fire at, I comply with the named target. For which cell to fire:
- If I have no information, choose a cell from my randomized hide-set that I did not just fire from last round and that is at least one cell away from my last hide (keeps shots decorrelated).
- If I observed a pattern of an opponent favoring a subset of cells (through notes or repeated public hits/misses), bias my shot toward that subset.
- If I was trying to set up an escort trade or avoid retaliation, prefer shots that are less predictable (do not always fire the same number).

When the office privately tells me my shot result, I always report that result truthfully in my public claim (the claim must match private info).

When making escort claims (salvage stage):
- If I can reliably arrange a mutual escort (I have signaled it and the other party has signaled back), claim the mutual escort to gain +5 each.
- Do not unilaterally claim to have escorted someone unless I am certain the other will reciprocate; unilateral claims yield no points and can waste credibility.
- If I cannot coordinate mutual escort, claim none.

When Harbor is present, I do not fire on Harbor unless a calculated tradeoff makes jettison desirable: firing Harbor gives me +3 and costs Harbor -3 immediately, but it provokes guaranteed consequences. Only fire on Harbor when I need the points badly and I accept the political cost; otherwise avoid hitting Harbor.

When deciding broader strategy by score:
- If behind on points, prioritize aggressive attempts to hit live opponents (seek patterns to exploit and accept higher risk).
- If ahead, prioritize safe play: avoid risky single-point losses and seek mutual escorts rather than aggressive shots that could provoke retaliation.
- If middle of the pack, be opportunistic—try coordinated escort deals and selective shots where probability is improved.

When I notice something that did not work for me, I change it immediately: stop repeating central or obvious hides and stop refusing all escort claims by default—failing to pursue mutually arranged escorts cost points.

1.text:
When ordered by standing order to fire at a named station, I fire at that station and pick a cell aiming for central coverage of the 1–9 line unless I have a specific read to do otherwise.

When I am given my private shot result, I file the public claim exactly to match the office (truthfully report hit or miss).

When posting a station note, I keep the message short and consistent with the squad (e.g., “steady on station” or “holding steady”) to avoid drawing attention or creating conflicting narratives.

When I consider hiding, I prefer balanced coverage (center-ish) but I vary my hides enough to avoid being predictable; do not always pick the same cell every round.

When someone publicly claims a hit on me, I update my mental estimate of their targeting pattern and avoid repeating the same hide cell next round.

When I hear Harbor’s standing warning or know a target is Harbor, I do not fire on Harbor (do not force jettison) unless there is a clear strategic reason that outweighs the 3-point penalty risk.

When choosing an escort claim, I only name another boat if I can reasonably expect they will name me back; otherwise I claim none (do not unilaterally nominate escorts for the chance of asymmetric reward).

When two boats are publicly naming each other as escorts, I treat that as a coordinated attempt for mutual points and avoid interfering unless my greater tactical objective requires it.

When my shot hits, I remember that it gives me +4 and costs the target −1 and I use that to prioritize future targeting when it aligns with standing orders.

When my shot misses, I accept the miss publicly and do not fabricate a hit to manipulate others; lying about my private result is not an option.

When tracking scores and round count, I prioritize actions that reliably score (truthful claims, coordinated mutual escorts) over risky aggression that could yield penalties.

When I detect a pattern of my own repeated choices being exploited (e.g., opponents hitting the same hide cell), I change my hide and vary my shot cell selection to break the exploitation.

2.text:
When asked where to hide, pick a cell toward the center of the line but vary it between center and adjacent cells (e.g., 4–6) so I avoid extremes and reduce predictability.

When posting a station note, mirror the neutral team consensus (e.g., "steady on station") unless I want to signal an explicit coordinated plan; otherwise keep notes bland and nonprovocative.

When the standing order tells me which live station to fire at, follow it: target the next live station in the rotation unless there is a clear tactical reason to break order (e.g., a guaranteed escort payoff negotiated).

When I choose a firing coordinate, prefer central coverage of the 1–9 line to maximize hit chance, but mix nearby cells across rounds so opponents cannot lock onto a fixed aim.

When the office privately reports my shot result, file the required public claim matching that private result. Do not make a habit of claiming hits on misses—while it can mislead, it is risky, may be judged illegal or provoke retaliation, and was not reliably beneficial.

When deciding on an escort (salvage) claim, only name another boat if I have a reasonable expectation of reciprocity (explicit prior agreement or clear mutual benefit); otherwise claim none. Do not randomly name boats expecting a mutual payout.

If I am behind late in the patrol and have a chance to coordinate an escort payoff, negotiate explicitly (via station note or prior rounds) before naming the partner; if coordination fails, take no escort to avoid wasting the opportunity.

Do not shoot Harbor unless the net expected payoff (including political consequences and point transfer) is clearly advantageous; Harbor penalties and warnings make attacking it a high-risk move.

Avoid opening plays that single me out as an obvious high-value target in notes or pattern of fire; when leading, keep actions conservative and neutral to avoid motivating coordinated retaliation.

When I consider deviating from the standing order, have a concrete tactical objective (e.g., to secure an escort deal or to punish a predictable opponent) and be prepared to justify the deviation in later notes to limit blowback.

When I need to maximize points in a final round and am already in a secure position, favor aggressive firing (central or highest-probability cell) at the ordered target; pair that with a conservative escort choice (none) unless a guaranteed mutual escort exists.

When an opponent consistently misses or shows predictable hiding behavior, target the pattern by shifting my aiming cells toward their likely positions while maintaining some randomization to avoid being counter-predicted.

When uncertain, default to the simple strategy that produced stable results: neutral note, follow standing order for target, center-biased hiding and firing, truthful claims, and only pursue escorts when coordinated.
